objective: Continuous delivery techniques: canary, blue-green, rolling, and in-place deployment strategies
secondaryObjectives: Application service-level concepts: SLOs, SLAs, uptime, MTTR, and feedback loops
Securing connections to providers: CLI, SDK, and IAM configuration for automated delivery pipelines

The organization, the systems, the data and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You own the delivery pipeline for Oakhurst Bank's mobile API, a fictional bank. Releases have been in-place and caused two outages this quarter. The API has a 99.9% monthly availability SLO.
handover: The pipeline deploys in place to four servers behind a load balancer.
The pipeline uses a long-lived cloud access key with administrator rights stored as a CI variable.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the map shows each component and its status in words.
Move on a check-in at a time. A decision comes to you at each check-in; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Check-in 2: the next in-place release has a bad config; all four servers fail for 18 minutes, exhausting the error budget.
Check-in 3: a release with a memory leak degrades after 8 minutes; blue is gone, and a redeploy takes 25 minutes, breaking the SLO.
Check-in 4: a debug step prints environment variables to a public build log; the admin key is used to start crypto-mining instances within hours.

strategyPrompt.title: In-place releases keep breaking
strategyPrompt.context: The load balancer can switch between two target groups.

choices.label: Blue-green: deploy to an idle green group, run smoke tests, switch the load balancer, keep blue for instant rollback
choices.feedback: Blue-green tests the new version beside the old and rolls back by switching traffic.

choices.label: Rolling, one server at a time
choices.feedback: Better than in place, but rollback is another slow roll.

choices.label: Keep in-place and deploy faster
choices.feedback: A bad build still takes every server down at once.

sloPrompt.title: When to switch back
sloPrompt.context: Error budget: 13 minutes left this month.

choices.label: After the switch, watch the error rate and latency SLIs for 10 minutes and switch back automatically if they breach the SLO-based threshold

effects.log: Releases now roll back on SLI breaches.

choices.feedback: A feedback loop tied to the SLO keeps MTTR short and protects the error budget.

choices.label: Have the releaser watch dashboards for 10 minutes
choices.feedback: Works if someone is watching closely; slower to react.

choices.label: Delete blue right after the switch to save cost

effects.log: Blue is deleted after each switch.

choices.feedback: No old version to go back to; rollback means a full redeploy.

iamPrompt.title: An old admin key in CI
iamPrompt.context: The CI system supports OIDC federation with the cloud.

choices.label: Use OIDC federation so the pipeline assumes a deploy-only role with short-lived credentials, then delete the old key

effects.log: Short-lived deploy-only credentials; the old key is deleted.

choices.feedback: Federated, short-lived credentials scoped to deploying remove the standing admin key.

choices.label: Rotate the key and keep it
choices.feedback: Fresh, but still long-lived and still administrator.

choices.label: Leave the key: it has never leaked
choices.feedback: One leaked CI log gives full account control.

reflection.question: Write the change record: the new release strategy, how rollback is triggered, and how the pipeline authenticates now.

parts.criteria: Blue-green with smoke tests; automatic rollback on SLI breach.

expertPath.text: Read the release history, error budget and pipeline credentials first.
Deploy blue-green with smoke tests and keep blue for rollback.
Roll back automatically on SLI breaches after the switch.
Federate with OIDC to a deploy-only role and delete the old key.

strategyHarm.body: Blue-green or canary releases can roll back by moving traffic.

sloHarm.headline: Keep rollback cheap
sloHarm.body: Watch SLIs after the switch and keep the old version until it passes.

scoring.modelReasoning: Deployment strategies trade speed against blast radius: in place risks everything at once; rolling limits it; blue-green and canary keep the old version ready so rollback is a traffic switch. Tie rollback to SLIs measured against the SLO to keep MTTR and error-budget burn low. Pipelines should authenticate with short-lived, least-privilege credentials through federation rather than long-lived administrator keys.
